description: Hi! I’m a curious and enthusiastic learner who loves exploring space, technology, AI, and new ideas. I enjoy storytelling, communication, brainstorming, and turning interesting ideas into meaningful projects. I’m looking to build a team where we can learn from each other, experiment, and create something impactful for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
TransitNet is a deep-learning tool that tells real exoplanet transits apart from look-alike false positives in NASA Kepler data. When a planet crosses in front of its star, the star’s light dips slightly. But eclipsing binary stars, stellar variability and instrument artifacts can produce similar dips, and checking thousands of candidates by hand is slow and hard to scale.

We built a pipeline that takes Kepler light curves from NASA’s MAST archive and labels them using the NASA Exoplanet Archive’s Kepler Objects of Interest table, which separates confirmed planets from false positives. Each light curve is flattened, phase-folded on its orbital period, and binned into two views: a global view showing the full orbit and a local view zoomed in on the dip. A two-branch 1D convolutional neural network reads both views and outputs the probability that the signal is a real planet. To make the results trustworthy, we added Grad-CAM explanations that highlight which part of the light curve drove each decision, plus a helper that lets anyone vet a Kepler star by name.

TransitNet speeds up the triage of candidate signals and helps scientists focus on the most promising planets. It is inspired by the deep-learning work behind the discovery of Kepler-90i, the eighth planet in its system.
details:
What it does and how it works
TransitNet is a deep-learning tool that decides whether a dip in a star’s brightness is caused by a real planet. NASA’s Kepler mission recorded thousands of such dips, but many are false positives such as eclipsing binary stars, stellar variability and instrument artifacts. Checking them by hand is slow. We take Kepler light curves from NASA’s MAST archive and label them using the NASA Exoplanet Archive’s Kepler Objects of Interest table (confirmed planets vs false positives). Each light curve is flattened and phase-folded on its orbital period, then binned into two views: a global view of the full orbit, and a local view zoomed in on the dip. A two-branch 1D convolutional neural network reads both views and outputs the probability that the signal is a real planet. The global view helps catch secondary eclipses that give away binary stars, and the local view helps tell a planet’s flat-bottomed dip from a binary’s V-shaped one.

Benefits and intended impact
TransitNet speeds up the triage of candidate signals so scientists can focus on the most promising planets. Grad-CAM explanations show which part of the light curve drove each prediction, so researchers can check the model’s reasoning instead of trusting a black box. Anyone can also vet a Kepler star by name using a built-in period search followed by the CNN. The long-term goal is faster, more transparent exoplanet candidate screening.

Tools and technology
Python, PyTorch, scikit-learn, NumPy, Matplotlib and the lightkurve package. Data came from NASA Kepler (MAST archive) and the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Development and training were done in Jupyter and Google Colab, and the code is open source on GitHub at https://github.com/BhavishyasriMatangi-rgb/kepler-transit-cnn.

Creativity
Instead of only building a classifier, we combined a two-view CNN with explainability and a vet-any-star feature. We also built a physics-based synthetic light-curve generator, with U-shaped planet transits and V-shaped eclipsing binaries that include secondary eclipses, so the whole pipeline can be demonstrated offline. The approach is inspired by the deep-learning work behind the discovery of Kepler-90i.

Factors we considered
We handled class imbalance (far more false positives than planets) with a weighted loss and augmentation, and we dealt with noisy, gappy light-curve data through flattening and binning. We focused on explainability so results can be checked, and we avoid overclaiming by evaluating only on held-out test data. Current limitations are that the model is trained on a subset of Kepler objects and does not yet use centroid or odd-even depth inputs. Extending it to TESS data is future work.

Use of AI
AI assistance (Claude) was used to help write the code and documentation, and I reviewed and ran the results ourselves.
